item.description: Franco Berardi begins by redefining the word.

item.title: Hauntology
item.description: The genre’s founding record predates its name by six years.

item.title: Fisher — Ghosts of My Life
item.description: Author: Mark Fisher Title: Ghosts of My Life: Writings on Depression, Hauntology and Lost Futures Year: 2014 Type: Essay collection (Zero Books; 2022 reissue with a new introduction) The book opens inside a canceled TV serial.

item.title: Bob Dylan
item.description: Bob Dylan arrived in New York in January 1961 as a nineteen-year-old from Hibbing, Minnesota, carrying an acoustic guitar and an encyclopedic knowledge of American folk, blues, and country music.

item.title: Brian Eno
item.description: On Roxy Music’s first two records there is an instrument the credits can’t quite name: the rest of the band, fed through Brian Eno’s synthesizer and sent back out transformed.

item.title: Carole King
item.description: The opening chord of “I Feel the Earth Move” is a left-hand piano pattern that could be R&B — percussive, rhythmically locked, the kind of figure that anchors a groove before a voice even arrives.

item.title: Muddy Waters
item.description: The voice is unhurried and half-spoken, sure of itself to the point of menace, a man stating his business and daring the room to disagree.

item.title: Phil Spector
item.description: Phil Spector is the first pop producer to matter as an auteur, the first to make the argument, through sheer sonic force, that the producer could be the primary author of a record.

item.title: Robert Johnson
item.description: Keith Richards first heard Robert Johnson at Brian Jones’s flat, on the one record player, and asked the obvious question: “Who is the other guy playing with him?” There was no other guy.
